utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to continue the examination of witness Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radic. Please be seated. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given -- I said good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... come to you over the ground but I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday you addressed the issue of the power and influence of the deputies in the Krajina, and you mentioned some of the factors that produced that power and influence. One of the factors you mentioned was their linkage to the leadership and their ability to convey to people in the Krajina, and people on the ground generally, the decisions that had been made in the Assembly and by the leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, is it also correct that in addition to conveying the official decisions, which were available in the Official Gazette, for example, that the deputies were in a position to convey their discussions and meetings with members of the leadership, and therefore, to convey how decisions and orders were to be implemented and which were the most important?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could, but they didn't actually have to. In fact, if I received a document, it would be quite clear to me how I was to implement what was in it. Although some people did try and do their best to explain what we were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But it's correct, isn't it, that one of the factors that led to the deputies' view of themselves as more important than the municipal leaders was their proximity to the leadership and their ability to convey priorities and the manner in which orders should be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the questioning this morning is starting off in an extremely leading form in an area which is not justified. It's not as if the particular difficulties which lead to more flexibility in the manner of questioning arise in relation to this sort of matter, because they plainly don't. Leaving aside the fact that there's a considerable amount of repetitiveness involved here. This is really Mr. Tieger setting out the propositions that eventually he would like to appear somewhere in submissions made by the Prosecution in relation to this case. So, just seeking the witness's rubber stamp to what he's saying. These are simply, plainly leading questions, which shouldn't be presented in this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the suggestion that I'm in a position to seek a rubber stamp from Mr. Radic or any other witness of this type I think is clearly inaccurate. Furthermore, that's not remotely what I'm attempting to do. I am putting appropriate propositions to this witness, some of which may appear self-evident to the Defence, but nevertheless should be addressed in court. Now, if those are put in the form of more pointed questions, directing the witness's attention to the precise issues that need to be addressed, I think that's perfectly appropriate with such a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're directed to avoid repetitious elements. The Chamber found some. And I wouldn't say not -- that you would not be allowed to lead at all, but a bit less would certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, with that guidance from the Court, let me reconfigure the question slightly, but I still would like to address some of those issues. Yesterday you indicated that the deputies would convey the orders and decisions that had been made in Pale, and with the expectation that they would be implemented. Was it also understood by the people on the ground that the deputies would convey back to Pale the extent to which those instructions were implemented on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two questions there. The first is whether they conveyed the decisions to us, which we later received in written form, and to that question I have to say that things like that did happen, although because they arrived before the written decisions arrived. And anybody who received this, if I can call it, a priori information would listen to it, because these were new things coming down to us, being conveyed to us. And quite certainly, they did take back to Pale, convey to Pale, how things were being implemented on the ground and what we thought about them. Because, after all, they were popular deputies, deputies of the people, and it was a good idea for them to see and hear what the people thought and convey it back to Pale. So in brief, that would be my answer to those questions of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition to the factors which you've identified that generated the power and influence of the deputies in the region, is it also correct that part of their power was derived from the fact that they had a powerful leader?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's in the realm of conjecture and surmise whether the leader was powerful or not powerful. He was president of the Assembly. What he told them, I really can't say. All I can do is assume, just as you can assume what he might have said. And most probably he did issue certain information which was conveyed to us on the ground. Now, what it was that he told them, I really can't speculate. I wasn't there. I didn't attend the meetings of the People's Assembly. So I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take this proposition one step at a time, Mr. Radic. You would agree that the power of someone in the local region would be enhanced by that person's connection with a powerful figure at the Republic level; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can I say? You know, sir, if you convey a certain amount of authority to an individual, then it is this conveyance of authority, and quite obviously, then, that individual would enjoy respect among the populace. And ultimately, those of us who were there to implement things on the ground, we too had to have a certain amount of authority and respect because this authority was conveyed to us. He conveys something to the people on the ground, and this could be done by somebody placed in a higher position. Now, of course, information was conveyed orally, not only by telephone and telefax, because it was wartime, so it was by word of mouth as well. And of course, power could have been derived from there too, in the eyes of the people and in our own eyes in the Municipal Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And applying that principle to the deputies of 1992, it's correct, isn't it, that their power in the region was enhanced by the perception of their connection to a powerful figure --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're back to just distinctly leading questions. This really is in the form of propositions in the Prosecution's case presented to the witness, even leaving aside the fact that some of it seems to be just such blindingly obvious common sense in the world that one could hardly need a witness to say that connections with one person might enhance something with somebody else and so on. But the last question is simply a leading question designed to get the witness's approval to the proposition formulated for him, which is what a leading question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the questions are of a quite leading character. It's also to some extent different from what is usually practiced in examination-in-chief. It seems that you find a reason to do it this way. If it is another relation with what you announced, then I think we should formalise that. If not, then you're directed to deal with the matter not in a similar leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would seek leave in this case, if such formal leave is necessary, but let me explain the genesis of that particular question and that and line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we do that in the presence of the witness or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I hesitate to take too much time, but since this is a general proposition that we'll be dealing with overall, perhaps the Court will allow me some latitude with this particular issue and not take it against my time with this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is a procedural issue which is not directly related to the examination of the witness. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, there's a procedural issue we'd like to discuss. Would you please be so kind to follow Madam Usher to leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A couple of points, Your Honour. First of all, the line of questioning arose, as the Court may recall, from comments by the witness in his interview that -- to the effect that one of the factors that made the deputies think of themselves as more important and more influential was that they had a masterful leader in Mr. Krajisnik. And I attempted to follow up on that comment to some extent today. I essentially asked the witness in a question that was not objected to and that seemed quite appropriate whether or not that was one of the factors that the deputies relied on to consolidate and enhance their own power, that is, their connection to a powerful leader, a fairly straightforward question which obviously was linked to the earlier inquiry. There was an evasive response that had -- that was very generalised, and I attempted to bring the witness back to it, first by seeking his general view on the issue of linkage and power and then turning him back to the same question I had asked him before, a question which was not objected to but which he didn't answer. I think that is an example of why leading questions in this context are both economical and appropriate. The witness and I could continue this dance for quite a while, but it seems to me it's far more productive to address the issue as directly as possible, which is what a so-called leading question does. It puts the proposition to the witness and asks him his position on it. Now, of course, when there's a witness closely identified with a party, there may be a risk that doing -- that conducting the examination that way or asking a question in that manner will suggest to the witness what he should answer, but in this context, where there is not only little risk of the witness doing so, but more of a risk that the witness is likely to give an answer contrary to what the examiner seeks, the prohibition against leading questions no longer has the force it does in other situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A number of simple points, Your Honour. First of all, yes, leading questions are nearly always going to be economical, but that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One could simply put the whole case to the witness and say please agree. So that's not really the point. The question is whether they are fair to be allowed. The second point is the fact that I may not object to a particular question doesn't amount to the slightest waiver of objections to other questions. I may have all sorts of reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- to one question but then objecting to something which seems similar. The -- so -- some of the questions which Mr. -- but I will say that one or two of the questions to which I did not object, the reason I didn't object was precisely because they were so general, and I'm entitled to form an assessment of what value they might or might not have if they're put in an extremely general form. But as far as this witness is concerned, it isn't -- we're not in an area where this witness has shown distinct hostility in a way that would conventionally then often lead to justification for something akin to cross-examination. It isn't that this witness, as I submit the Tribunal will have seen, it's not so much that this witness is distinctly evasive. We've seen a lot more evasive witnesses in this trial than this particular witness. In fact, the problem is to some extent the opposite, that when one looks at the tenor of the interviews, of which we have the transcripts and his evidence, the danger is this witness's slight readiness to agree to something, followed a little bit later perhaps by readiness to agree to something which contradicts to what he agreed to the first time round. So there is actually a strong danger in relation to this particular witness, and we've been very specific. It's very ad hominem here. This witness's particular approach to questioning and the way in which he gives his answers makes it especially important that so far as possible he is not led. If he does become directly evasive or if we get into a position there, then, when counsel feels that his answer can be in effect impeached by showing him some other material or some inconsistent statement he's made, that's a different situation and we deal with that as it arises. But in relation to this particular line of questioning, I simply adhere to my submission that we should not have leading questions here at this point in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think there are two problems. One of them, leading questions. The Chamber is not that much afraid that this witness will come up with answers just on the basis of your suggestions. So to that extent, the reasons for the -- perhaps I shouldn't say prohibition, because it's not a clear prohibition in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this Tribunal, but the reasons for not putting leading questions to the witness might not be as compelling as with some other witnesses. At the same time, the Chamber observes that the problems arise mainly in the field of where an opinion is asked about who got power and as soon as we leave the realm of facts, and that could contribute very much to the problems at this moment. If we ask a witness whether he considers that the power came from the air or from the ground, that's of course asking for opinion rather than asking about facts. And I think that what has been said about that yesterday in the testimony of the witness and on these aspects is already considerable. So you are -- the guidance of the Chamber is that you try to get back more to the facts, that we should not be that anxious about not leading the witness at all, but the Chamber has understood the position of the Defence also not to object to whatever leading questions. If you would keep that in the back of your mind, we could continue. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Radic. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, let me move on to a slightly different topic. When people on the ground disregarded or disobeyed orders, were they replaced or disciplined?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that I personally sometimes did not implement what I was told to do. I was not punished in any way, but things happened to me that would not have happened had I obeyed. There were removals, but I cannot tell you whether they were connected with the fact that these persons did not listen to what the deputies had said. There were removals, but now when I'm thinking about the motives behind it for the removals of some of the people in some -- working for some of the municipalities quite close to the town of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, when you were asked about this subject on July 28th, 2002, is it correct that you gave this response. Question on page 56, line 23 of the July 2002 interview: "When people disobeyed instructions from Pale within this region, were they generally removed?" Your answer: "Well, at least they would go through what I went through in S '93" - I presume that's September 93 - "they would be called in, they would go through ironing, but some of them would be replaced straight on." Question: "Ironing. You mean things would be straightened out with the person I don't know I --" Answer: "I was -- you know very well what ironing means" in inverted commas, "but it's not a tepid iron either; it's a very hot one." Mr. Radic, was that a correct answer and is it correct that when people disobeyed instructions from Pale within the Krajina, they were either replaced straight on or subjected to ironing, in inverted commas?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were replaced right away. Others were subjected to disciplinary procedure, or rather, as you would put it informally, ironing, in inverted commas, and then they would subsequently change their views. I hope that you're not expecting me to repeat verbatim what I said in July 2002, but I've given you the gist of it now and then. But some of those people were replaced, but I'm not sure whether it had anything to do with that. And of course, they were held responsible for what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that when you made -- first of all, during the course of your interviews with the Prosecutor, and obviously to some extent during your testimony here in court, you've acknowledged some of the bad things that happened in the Krajina. Did you also acknowledge in your previous interviews that you could have done more to prevent some of the bad things that happened but that you were under the control of your compatriots, and that prevented you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was present on all the three sides. You could help others only surreptitiously. This was never done in an overt manner, to help anyone, to enable him to leave a given territory. So you had to keep in mind what the populace thought of it, because there were many who arrived from Bugojno, Bihac, Zenica, and other towns who had been expelled from there. Of course I was very careful in assisting people, because I hardly expected anyone to commend me for such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that you had to work outside the existing political structure to try to help non-Serbs and that if you worked inside the structure, it would be dangerous for you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not only the political structure that was important there; it was also the general people, those who had been expelled could not understand why the people who were responsible for the expelling are to be assisted to leave the area. Therefore, it was not only a political view; it was the view of the people who had arrived there. Because there was some 15 to 20.000 people who had been expelled --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10 to 15.000 people who had been expelled from Bihac and Bugojno, and they were very sensitive to such issues, and of course I had to be very careful in taking any such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the problem was both the political structure itself and the -- what you call the general people; is that right? Is that what you're trying to explain?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We keep returning to the political structure. The political structures included the SDA, HDZ, and SDS. They all held identical views vis-a-vis the people that they did not advocate for. And it is quite certain that whatever I had done in that respect would not have been looked upon favourably by the political structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to understand your answer: That's part of an effort you made during your interviews, and also in court, to point out that things that were happening within the Serbian -- the Bosnian Serb political structures were, in your view, were also happening within the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat political structures; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you the following, sir: That many of the things that we were attributed as being the main players or actors of, these were things that were already done on the other sides, and I have to tell you this belatedly: Whatever happened in Republika Srpska had also happened previously in the other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I wanted to tell you also earlier on when I responded to your answers. And I will tell you that whatever the side we're talking about, the people who helped those who were not looked upon favourably in the particular area, these people exposed themselves to quite greater risk. I have to tell you, of course, that even on the other sides, there were people who were helping their neighbours, and even relatives, because there were many mixed marriages. And one could not avoid not helping persons coming from mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm a bit confused about both questions and answers, and perhaps you could seek clarification with the witness. You asked him about whether he acknowledged in the previous interviews that he could have done more to prevent some of the bad things. First of all, the bad things have not been specified. But that he was under the control of his compatriots, that kept him off from doing so. In questions and answers, it's quite unclear whether we're talking about helping specific individuals or helping groups, I would say masses rather than individual cases. I would like to know, first of all, what we understand by "bad things." Is that that one person was driven out of his area or helping an individual? Is that to allow him to leave the territory? It's all too vague for me at this moment. And I'm really confused about individuals or groups. Could you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the Court would like me to put some of those earlier questions in context. I asked you about your response to -- or the information you provided during the course of your interviews. During those interviews, you spoke about dismissals of non-Serbs, expulsions of non-Serbs, large-scale killings of non-Serbs. Were those the bad things that you were talking about when you indicated to the interviewers that there were more things that you might have done but for the fact that you were under the control of or pressure from your compatriots?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely as you've said now. Perhaps I could have done more, but that's what I think now, with hindsight. And now I wonder whether I could have done more. The Honourable Judge asked what these bad things were. Well, when you decide to move a person to another apartment, or when a person is left without a job, especially without any apparent reason. For instance, the differentiation case concerning the music teacher. Under the pretext of him having access to some information. He could only have had access to musical notes and not to any information of relevance to Republika Srpska. Of course, quite the other case is that of the postal workers or myself, as the president of the municipality. The same is true for the people who wished to join their families, and that's where I had to intervene, because I thought it very bad not to do that. Later it was different, because you had the Red Cross Committee that arrived there and helped families reunite. Now, when you mentioned mass-scale murders, in the town where I lived, there were no mass-scale murders, and this was proved. But, as I've said, wherever I could, I tried to use my influence to prevent such things from happening. Unfortunately, this was not within my competence. That's what these bad things were. When I'm looking at it now, with hindsight, it does seem to me that I could have done more. However, under those wartime conditions, it was very dangerous when you have refugees arriving from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina every day looking for safety in Banja Luka. It was very difficult to help non-Serbs keep their apartments from being taken by the Serbs who had been expelled from other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But this was a matter to be dealt with by the police. I tried at least to advocate for people of great repute who were university professors, of all ethnicities, and that's what I tried to do. And this is how I tried to answer the question about the bad things and about what I could have done or could not have done. Of course, had we not had the war, had we not had these people arriving from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were following closely what was going on, perhaps I could have done more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're talking about what you perhaps could have done, are you talking about intervening in favour of groups of the population or are you talking about intervening in favour of certain individuals that addressed you? So when you're talking about apartments, did you consider to intervene for all those who are not having apartments, or were you considering to intervene for a specific person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody intervened, Your Honour, for those who did not have any apartments. But for those who had them and who were supposed to be evicted in order for those who were expelled from other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be put up there. Now, if you are asking me about the specific groups, there was a group of Jews in Banja Luka who were already ready to leave Banja Luka for Tel Aviv. They applied to me. We met, and I took upon myself the responsibility of ensuring their safety. And they were safe throughout the war, and they are still in Banja Luka today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me bring you back to the example. When I said those without an apartment, I meant to refer to once they would be evicted. But about these apartments: If you considered to intervene, or when you are considering that you might have done more, is this because you should have protected those who were at a point to be evicted, or are you talking about individual cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they were not thrown out of their apartments into the streets. We had another euphemism that was called the rationalisation of housing space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please answer my question. My question was whether you're talking about -- I mean, the specific methods and where they were housed afterwards is not the issue. My issue -- I'm asking you whether you considered that you could have done more for the groups or just for individual cases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not have done more for the entire groups, simply because the position was that those who were arriving to Banja Luka, who had been expelled from other areas, had to be put up somewhere. Accommodation had to be found for them. And that is why the occupants of certain apartments were moved to other apartments. I tried to protect some of them and have them keep their apartments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did that in individual cases but not for the group as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't possible to do something of the sort for the entire group. Excluding this example that I've given of the group of Jews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And why was it not possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to tell you why not. But this was in fact not done by the authorities but by the companies, because they were owners of these apartments, and they were ordered that they had to carry out the rationalisation of housing space, give the apartments to families of fallen soldiers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ordered by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to tell you, but there has to be somewhere this document about the rationalisation of housing space. I know for a fact that this document did not originate from the Municipal Assembly that I presided. It had to have come from the authorities, and this document must be somewhere, because it was sent to all the companies that owned apartments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you said before that you were kept off from doing anything against the bad things because your compatriots - and let me just find the literal wording - yes, that you couldn't do anything because you were under the control of your compatriots, that kept you off from doing so. Is this an example where your compatriots kept you off from interfering at that moment with -- well, eviction of apartments and how it was all arranged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you. When someone arrives from a war theatre, it was difficult to prevent the person from doing anything. The police even could not prevent them from -- especially when they are armed, you could not prevent them from evicting people, to put some people who had arrived from Bugojno or elsewhere. Not even myself, as president of the Municipal Assembly, could not stand in front of these barrels and prevent them from doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that we have now two potential sources for eviction, one because the employers were ordered to evict people, and you now come with an answer which indicates that those who wanted to occupy those apartments would be armed, and therefore, no one could stop them, which of course are two different reasons. My question, however, was whether this whole, let's say, housing problem, was that an example of where compatriots kept you off from perhaps what you would have wished to do or which you would have thought was good to do in order to avoid the bad things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us start with employers. Employers had the task of providing for those who were in the war and for their families and who had no apartments. There was one such case where I prevented the eviction. There was a person coming to my office with a weapon. I said: Okay. I do agree for that particular person to keep their apartment, but give me another apartment. And I had no other apartment to provide them with. And there were also cases where employers are asked for apartments, but you also had people arriving from the front line who never even consulted the employers or the owners of the apartments. They would simply go armed to some of the apartments and asked the people who lived there to leave. And that was the case where a president of the Municipal Assembly could do nothing about. We had the ethnic Ukrainians there. They also asked for protection. There was quite a large group of ethnic Ukrainians there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have wished to prevent people coming armed to an apartment and kick those who are living there out by force of arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no such opportunity. They were not under my command or competence. But I did caution and warn the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you would have wished to prevent this to happen. Your answer was that you had no power to do that. My question was not whether you had any power. The question was whether you would have wished to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I wished to prevent that, because it was clear to me then that these were never to be their apartments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you said you warned the military authorities. What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could order them not to enter these apartments, but these were workers in the very companies that owned the apartment. So if the company itself had nothing against it, what could the military do there? Because it was the company giving them the apartment that they owned. The apartment that was at the time occupied by someone who was not at the front, unlike the person that was given the apartment. There were also Serbs who dodged these mobilisation call-ups who had to then move to smaller apartments, and then the families of soldiers would be given their apartments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say the military couldn't do anything about it. Why did you warn them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was warning about those who came by apartments in a different fashion, not this way. For instance, armed men entered one of the apartments, and that's where I asked for their assistance, and these people were then thrown out, because they had not entered the apartment pursuant to a company's orders or anybody else's orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer to my question what the military authorities did upon your warning is that they threw them out, those who had taken these apartments by force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In those cases where these people had not been given the apartments by companies or any other way, in such cases, these people were thrown out by the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the police in the military could do something under those circumstances. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just -- it goes back quite a long way, but I wanted, of course, to allow Your Honour's line of questioning to be completed. But way back at page 15, line 22 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't follow you, because I had a problem with my laptop and I have to borrow. Yes. You said page 15 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, line 22, Your Honour. There was a -- there's a passage which appears in the transcript as quite the other -- I hope I can be heard through the microphone. "Quite the other case is that of the postal workers or myself as the president of the municipality." Ms. Cmeric tells me that where it says "the postal workers or myself," there was actually something said rather more extensive in relation to the interception of communications, that there was perhaps a whole phrase or a whole point included in what the witness said there, which seems to have got dropped from the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that's too much to deal with at this very moment, but is it essential at this moment for the continuation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not really, Your Honour. Since we're pages on from it, it's probably inconvenient as Your Honour indicates. I didn't want it to slip by, because apparently it was quite a chunk that got dropped from the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The attention then is drawn that it should be checked on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's one other point. At page 19, line 25, the -- all I know is that the phrase is "I said." It's: "I said: Okay. I do agree for that particular person," and so on. Ms. Cmeric tells me it's "he said," not "I said."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That has to be checked. The attention has been drawn to it and if there's any need to correct that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you used a local police official, Mr. Tutus, I believe his name was, to assist you in efforts to minimise the evictions or expulsions of non-Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when the authorities in Pale found out that Mr. Tutus was helping you, he was replaced; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether when you say the authorities in Pale," you mean the Ministry of the Interior. If you do, then yes, he was replaced with the knowledge of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, in 1992 and -- well, in 1992, you knew that mosques were being destroyed in municipalities across the Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of destroying those mosques?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same purpose as destroying the Orthodox churches in Herceg-Bosna, for example, and Bosnia as well, for that matter, the same purpose, exactly the same: To wipe out the traces of the existence of the peoples whose churches they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to prevent them from returning; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The destruction of mosques wouldn't have prevented them from returning. That is the example of Kozarac, Janja, and all the other towns where the mosques were destroyed, Zvornik. New mosques were built and people returned, so that didn't prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's too late to object to the question because it's been given, but I would like to observe nevertheless that that question to prevent them from returning, what Mr. Tieger did then was, having not got the answer he was looking for he then by his next question in a blatantly leading form gave the witness the answer that he'd actually been looking for when he asked the previous question. It's too late now because it's done and one can't object in a split second sometimes, but I would ask through the Trial Chamber that this does not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is there any basis for the suggestion you put to the witness in the written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's precisely the point I was going to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, during your interview in July 2001 you were asked that same question I asked you. And if we turn to page 73, at line 7, the question by Ms. Korner was: "Right. What I want to know is what was the purpose as you understood it of destroying mosques?" And your answer was: "Same as the destruction of Orthodox churches. To destroy the faith so that people wouldn't go back." That was the -- and then there's something unintelligible, "destroy the spiritual basis and they won't be coming back. It's crazy."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes. And just how crazy it was has been borne out by practice today, that new mosques are built, the Muslims are coming back, new Catholic churches are being built. The only thing is that in Herceg-Bosna the Orthodox churches are not being rebuilt. Very few are being rebuilt in Croatia, whereas a large number were destroyed. So that's why I called it crazy. And it proved to be just that. And you know yourself full well that I myself, immediately after the destruction of two mosques, two old mosques in Banja Luka I convened a press conference and you know what I said on the occasion. And it wasn't greeted with applause, let me tell you. You can be quite sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you've made the point before that Banja Luka was the last place in Republika Srpska where mosques were destroyed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And until the time that the mosques in Banja Luka were finally destroyed in 1993, you were always being told that this was your fault, isn't that right, and asked how you could allow a mosque to stand in Banja Luka when everywhere else there was not a single mosque left?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the people who were objecting that you were permitting or that Banja Luka still had mosques standing when all the others were down included those in the highest authority; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were people in whose towns, in the places they lived in, there were no more mosques left standing. And it was a thorn in their eye that here the mosques did exist. Of course, there were those who were attached to the higher echelons of government. I said attached to the higher echelons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the way in which this witness's evidence is being approached and the submissions made by the Prosecution, I submit that it's not -- this is not a witness where points such as the one I'm about to make should be left to cross-examination to clear up. When Mr. Tieger says to the witness by way of a question: "And the people who were objecting that you were permitting or that Banja Luka still had mosques standing when all the others were down included those in the highest authority; correct," it is only fair in the presentation of this case and it is only fair in the presentation of the Prosecution case that Mr. Tieger, so far as possible, is specific in relation to such matters. So rather than leave it to me for cross-examination, at this point, we submit that Mr. Tieger should be invited to make it clear in such questions who he is suggesting, if he is able to make a suggestion, or if not, to invite the witness to make clear who gave -- made any such statements. Because otherwise we've got -- we know what the case is about, and there's no reason for me to be secretive or to disguise this even in the witness's presence. Some label like the higher echelons or top leadership is brought into the question, and we know who is then going to be embraced in that very general, broad phrase in the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you're referring in your question to the highest authority, then it certainly would assist the Chamber to further explore what the basis of the knowledge of the witness is and whether he could give any further specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, with respect, Your Honour, I would say that objection was a bit premature in the course of this examination. I had just asked the first question on that subject, and I was moving on. However, I -- in this instance, I'm pleased to identify the source of those questions immediately, and we can move on from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it's difficult for Mr. Stewart, and for the Chamber as well, to know exactly what's going to happen next, but this would cause us to be hesitant to interfere when it's not yet clear that specification that the Defence or the Chamber would consider important still could come. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in light of that, Mr. Radic, let me turn your attention to some exchanges during the course of the interview in July, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make it clear. It's not the source. Mr. Tieger sought to answer my point there by saying that he was going on to identify the source of the questions. That was not the substance of my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The substance was that -- well, let me paraphrase it. If you say from whom did you get orders, from -- if the answer would be from important people, that would not assist unless you know who are important people. But I do agree with Mr. Stewart that when you're referring to the source, it was not a matter of a source but of course the source could lead us to the specification. So to that extent, Mr. Stewart, you could have waited for a while to see whether it was just source or sources which would give an entry to further specification. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I could have taken that risk, Your Honour, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're guided.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at page 73 of the July 2001 interview, you indicated that, as we discussed earlier, that mosques were being destroyed, what the reason for that was, and further, that you tried to prevent mosques from being destroyed and that people asked you -- people complained to you about that. And then at line 26, Ms. Korner asked you: "Okay. But who was talking to you about blowing up mosques?" And your answer was: "You're asking me who said it. Everybody, even those in the highest authority. There was complaining. They said, they always said "Radic, Banja Luka is fine. You're doing well. The only problem is you still have the mosques there. And, but -- and the first thing that I took the last USSR ambassador to see when he -- just before USSR fell apart, the first thing I took, first thing I showed him was the Ferhat Pasa Mosque because it was a building under UNICEF [sic] protection and it was one of the greatest treasures we had in Banja Luka." Ms. Korner continued: I'm sorry, I still want to ask you this you said people higher up were talking to you about destruction of the mosques. Who do you mean by people higher up?" And you said: "They didn't talk about the destruction as much as objecting to me for having -- for still having mosques a year after they were all destroyed. They all said it. And don't ask me for names. From the highest authority all the way down to the lowest." And Ms. Korner asked you: "All right does it include Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik?" Mr. Radic said: "They are wise enough not to say it out loud but they had their emissaries who said it all the time and one of them was especially persistent." And then you were asked who that was and you said: "Ask the CSB and ask the judges. They know everything." And she continued to press you: "Mr. Radic, I mean if you don't want to tell us, you don't have to but we'd like to have who you say Karadzic and Krajisnik sent as an emissary. Again you said again: "You're asking me to rat on people." And she said: "I am. I am so, Mr. Radic, you were prepared to talk to us because you wanted to assist us. It's clearly important who was sending whom Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were sending to say that the mosques should be destroyed." And you said: "I don't know if they sent them here, but Velibor Ostojic was on my back all the time." And then you explained, when asked: "He was like a political commissioner in the old Russian sense of the word. He was from Foca. He was -- he held a high position." Those answers were correct, isn't that right, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were being --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to say that I can't be certain -- all right, if that's what it says. Although I noticed, I did note that there were some errors, some mistakes. But I'm not sure I said -- I actually said that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik did that. But if it says so there, let it stand. Because the person who came didn't come without the knowledge of others, without anybody's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- Mr. Tieger, could you please -- perhaps I'll do it my myself. You said, but if it says so here, let it stand. Because the person who came, I take it that's Mr. Ostojic, didn't come without the knowledge of others, without anybody's knowledge. Who did you have in mind when you said that he didn't come without the knowledge of others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a general climate that prevailed, a general mood, and the result of that mood was the destruction of every mosque until the day the Banja Luka -- up until the Banja Luka mosque. So those who didn't react to the destruction of other mosques had to agree to his instructions, the instructions he gave in other towns and in Banja Luka as well. Now, who those were who gave him what they gave him, I don't know. I can't say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you said that he didn't come without the knowledge of others, you certainly would not have had in mind a local cab driver or -- I mean, what did you have in mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody who had to have been higher up in hierarchical terms than him. Because if I said what I said, then he was only the political commissar, secretary, who conveyed the party positions. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that with others, you meant others in a hierarchical higher position than he was, and he is then Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, as indicated in previous questions, the purpose, the intent of destroying the mosques was to -- in part, to discourage people of that ethnicity from returning and the purpose of destroying the mosques was to keep Muslims permanently out of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated my opinions about views of this kind and efforts of that kind. Unfortunately, in practice today, we see that Sarajevo is a Muslim city, thanks to the enormous number of mosques that have been built, which means that that concept and that philosophy is still in place on the soil of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Ferhat Pasa's mosque is a case in point, other mosques have been built, rebuilt, and people are coming back. So it was crazy, as I said, just as it was crazy to think that once you take over somebody else's apartment that it will be yours for all times. And now we see that 95 per cent of the apartments have been returned to their previous owners of non-ethnic Serbs in Banja Luka, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic ever complain to you that Banja Luka had not been properly cleansed, that is, that there were still Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two of them never did, never directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it didn't -- again, it didn't matter in that particular case, because of the answer the witness gave and was in fact likely to give. But I do suggest that questions of this sort, if they are coming up again, shouldn't present Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, as far as possible, as a package in this way. So that if a similar question does arise, more care should be taken not to package them together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is in the negative, so there's still a possibility to do that. Mr. Tieger, you are invited to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not asking for repetition of this question, Your Honour. There's no problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not repetition. It's a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wanted to make that clear. I'm not inviting this question to be redone in any different form. It's an indication of a flaw in that question which I'm submitting should not appear in other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But of course... Mr. Radic, the question was put to you whether Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic ever complained to you that Banja Luka had not been properly cleansed. Your answer was that two of them never did, never directly. Did they ever come one by one, just Mr. Karadzic, just Mr. Krajisnik, and complain to you, by whatever means, in a meeting, in a telephone conversation, by letter, by telefax, by -- to complain about Banja Luka not being properly cleansed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. I would have to remember a letter, a fax, a telephone conversation, or remarks of that kind by either one of them, either individually or together. I would have to have remembered that. But if there is a document in which it says so, I'd like to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... meeting? Because you did not mention a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither at a meeting, no. There was no mention of that, of the fact that Banja Luka would have to do the job or to give me instructions to do that. And I must say that I would have refused, quite certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. I found some similarity in their last question if I compare it with page 75 of an interview. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you say that you can't remember and would like to see a document which says so. Let me direct your attention to page 75 of the interview that was conducted in July of 2001. And beginning at line 21, you were asked by Ms. Korner: "Was there a meeting at some stage in Banja Luka between you and Karadzic and Krajisnik, when Karadzic was saying to you that Banja Luka hadn't been properly ethnically cleansed? In other words, they were blaming you that there were still Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka." Your answer was: "That was not just once; that happened a lot. But I can't recall exactly when they said all that, but that objection was made against me." And just a bit later in the interview, that point is raised again, and Ms. Korner says: "I'm sorry, I asked --" this is at page 76, beginning at line 4. "I'm sorry. I absolutely accept what you say that a large number of Serb refugees came to Banja Luka but you've told us that Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic complained on a number of occasions that you didn't cleanse Banja Luka of the Muslims and Croats. Therefore, it follows, Mr. Radic, does it not, that that was what they wanted to happen?" And then you go on to say: "As I say -- as I said, this would not have happened if we were not under such pressure. I would not have even allowed it to happen when it did if Banja Luka had not been under such pressure with so many refugees who were -- who saw Banja Luka as their haven, safe haven. Let me just tell you something if you're interested..." and you go on to talk about a document between Mr. Sommaruga and Mr. Koljevic entitled "The document on the voluntary departure of non-Serb population from Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're invited to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, does that refresh your recollection about a meeting or meetings between you, Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Krajisnik during which they complained that Banja Luka hadn't been properly ethnically cleansed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document means nothing to me, in view of the fact that it's all in English. There's no Serbian translation. But what I can see here is some passages that you read out, but this isn't a continuation of the question referring to the mosques. It doesn't follow on from that. We have now moved on to another area, if I -- and that's the question of ethnic cleansing. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is -- I think that's clear, Mr. Radic, that we are talking about a meeting during which Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik complained to you about ethnic cleansing and their complaint was that Banja Luka had not been properly ethnically cleansed. That is the subject, and that is the question.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we're done with the mosques, are we? We've finished with that question and we're now moving on to the question of ethnic cleansing as a continuation of the mosques topic. Once again, I have the English in front of me, so I can't really follow it that well. But what I said, I said fairly -- we went through it fairly quickly. You read it out fairly quickly. And at one point I saw the names Krajisnik, Karadzic and that Karadzic told me and not Krajisnik. You can look back to the text. That the proper ethnic cleansing hadn't been conducted. So it wasn't Krajisnik in that instance. There were objections all the time, criticisms all the time. You, I'm sure, have the intercept of the conversation between Mr. Brdjanin and the -- and President Karadzic, and he's complaining that I was dismissing Muslim managers -- that I was not dismissing Muslim managers. So I had objections of that kind and criticisms made of me of that kind on many occasions and as I said it was difficult to protect those people because there were quite of a lot that didn't agree with a policy of that kind, that people shouldn't be allowed to remain in Banja Luka, for instance. And the largest portion of the conversation with [indiscernible], which is something is doesn't say here, is that the majority of Muslims and Croats left after the ethnic cleansing of Krajina and the 450.000 people who passed through Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock and at the same time I'm looking at some of the comments by Mr. Radic, who says I can't follow it because I've got an English text in front of me. I take it that the interview was recorded in the original language used and that was B/C/S, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. The interviews were conducted in -- well, in both. Conducted in English, translated into B/C/S during the course of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So finally the tape could give confirmation of whether the transcript is correct. But I have first one additional question to you, Mr. Radic. You have drawn our attention to the fact that you said: Where I saw the names Karadzic and Krajisnik, that Karadzic was saying that Banja Luka hadn't been properly ethnically cleansed, and not Mr. Krajisnik. Did you want to draw our attention to the fact that that is what this text says, or did you want to draw our attention to that was actually the case, that is, that Mr. Karadzic said it and not Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what it says in written form, Your Honour, in the letter that -- or rather, interview which the Prosecutor placed before me here in English. I can follow English that much. It says Krajisnik and Karadzic said. That's what it said. So one of them said this, and that one was Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree that Mr. Tieger did not reflect properly, specifically on this part, and where you said, Mr. Tieger -- let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, since it's apparent that we must be approaching the break, because otherwise tapes run out, the transcripts of this interview does exist in B/C/S. We've got it. Ms. Cmeric has got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't got it. Perhaps the witness could read it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One of the reasons we haven't got it, Your Honour, probably you and I, is because it's of limited value to us. But to Ms. Cmeric, it's far more valuable. The witness has already referred, and quite fairly, we suggest, to difficulties about the fact that he's only been presented with it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have an opportunity then to give a B/C/S text over the break so that Mr. Radic can read it. And Mr. Tieger, where I said that you did not reflect the interview properly, it was -- you said: "I think it's clear, Mr. Radic, that we are talking about a meeting during which Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik complained to you about." Whereas the interview says that there was a meeting with the two of them in which Mr. Karadzic said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I fully accept that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, there is a B/C/S version of this interview. Would you be willing to read that over during the next break so that we are not stuck with the problem that you have an English text in front of you? And then I take it -- who will provide the B/C/S text? I haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll take that responsibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll take the responsibility. And could we then invite the witness to ask specific pages, because 75 pages is a bit much. I do not know where that appears in the B/C/S version. But could you identify, well, let's say two or three pages where this matter arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We obviously want to cut it down. Your Honour, we were only going to say if there is any difficulty at all, we do have clean B/C/S copies so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it your copies are clean as well, Mr. Stewart. If not, please take the ones --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, just contact us any time. We'll be in Defence counsel's room. So we can help on this straight away. Your Honour, while I'm on my feet, could I just mention there was an interpretation point at page 35, line 9. What appeared in English transcript: "So it wasn't Krajisnik in that instance." And then there was or were -- objection was the next sentence with that lead-in, so page 35, line 9. "So it wasn't Krajisnik in that instance." Ms. Cmeric assures me that there was no Serbian or B/C/S phrase from which that instance is derived, that in the witness's evidence, it simply was: So it wasn't Krajisnik. Full stop. And then the next sentence continued. In that instance, certainly has a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- implication in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It sounds logical, but of course we could check the original B/C/S tape whether it's -- what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And another point, Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note they might not have been in that instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further points?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid I've misnoted it. It was after that, so it was quite recently. There was a phrase ethnic cleansing of Krajina. So I've just lost the line reference. Ms. Cmeric will probably find it very quickly. It's 35, 19, the previous one was 35, 19, 35,19. And in fact it was ethnic cleansing of Knin Krajina and the Knin has got dropped there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. I think it's not essential for the answer. It was just an explanation the witness gave. So I take it that there's no problem with this understanding of his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I think it makes sense in context as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Radic, you're invited to read the couple of pages that will be provided to you during the break and we'll have a break of 25 minutes, until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Radic into the courtroom. Mr. Radic, did you have an opportunity to read the part of your 2002 interview relevant to the questions put to you just prior to the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it was 2001, that particular interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that it was the 2000 and -- but if so -- yes. But then just to defend myself, Mr. Tieger, if you look at the top of the page 75, you'll find the 16th of July, 2002, as in all the other pages, where it should read in the header 2001. So that was perhaps the reason for my mistake. But did you have an opportunity to read it again, Mr. Radic, or read it? I don't know whether it's the first time or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I had seen it, I probably forgot all about it. But now I have read through it carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radic, does that refresh your recollection about a meeting or meetings with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic during which Mr. Karadzic complained that Banja Luka had not been properly ethnically cleansed, that is, that there were still Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of ethnic cleansing was raised, was put by Ms. Korner, but later on she re-termed it into "deportation." They also insisted on the transportation having been carried out by cars, which wasn't true, and I corrected it later on. But however, here, Ms. Korner puts a question: Was it Karadzic who told you that Banja Luka had not been ethnically cleansed? And then I said that it wasn't that Karadzic had told me, but she put Karadzic into her question. And then I said that it wasn't on numerous occasions, and I don't recall Krajisnik having said it. But I have read through this carefully. You have suggested certain things to me. You were aware that the creation of your state involves deportation, and I said: "No, that is not true." One should also -- keep one in mind under 24, again Karadzic and Krajisnik that you hadn't cleansed Banja Luka sufficiently. Your Honour, these questions were put to me because my vice-president of the Municipal Assembly was a Muslim. The vice-president of the Executive Committee was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you are explaining a lot to us now, why questions were put to you. The first simple question is: You were asked, according to this transcript, whether there was a meeting at some stage in Banja Luka between you and Karadzic and Krajisnik, when Mr. Karadzic said something. Your answer was: "That was not just once. That happened a lot. But I can't really exactly -- recall exactly when they said all that, but that objection was made against me." That was your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is now seeking confirmation of this answer. So the first question is: Was there a meeting with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were. I cannot recall how many, but there was no mention of ethnic cleansing, but rather of -- about what was the number of Croats and Muslims who took part in the government. But yes, there were meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- was it that Mr. Karadzic at that moment addressed what you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot say for a fact whether it was him who spoke, but there was no mention of ethnic cleansing, but merely of the representation of different ethnicities in the government. These later questions put by Ms. Korner show the quintessence of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said -- but it was a meeting with Mr. -- several meetings with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic in Banja Luka; is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no specific meetings between me, Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Krajisnik. It must have been some other meeting, perhaps a session of the assembly or some other meeting where I had occasion to speak to them. But as for having separate meetings, including me, Mr. Karadzic, and Krajisnik on such an issue, there were no such meetings. Otherwise, there were meetings, but how many and when, I cannot recall. It was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're talking about the Assembly, did you mean the Banja Luka, the Municipal Assembly, or do you mean any other assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was customary for the Assembly to be convened always in a different town, in order for the deputies to be close to the people, in Banja Luka, Sanski Most, Bijeljina, Zvornik, Pale. But mostly at Pale. And whenever they would come to Banja Luka, that's when we would have occasion to see each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you said the Assembly, you meant the Republika Assembly and not the local assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No. Not the local.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just find another ... Yes. You are referring to a meeting where objections were made in respect of Muslims and Croats still in the government. Could you tell us how many there still were at the time of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, in the parliament, there was the group of SDA deputies, a group of the HDZ deputies. And as for the executive government, I told you that my vice-president of the Municipal Assembly was a Muslim. And the vice-president of the Executive Committee was Antun Ruzic, a Croat. And the chief of the inspectorate was Mr. Kustric, a Muslim. And at lower municipal levels there were still Muslims and Croats holding their positions. This could not have been the case at the time in Federation and in Herceg-Bosna. And that's what I was criticised for, for not having done otherwise. And if I may, if you allow, Your Honour, I would like to add the following: The distribution of power was done according to the election results. And Banja Luka had a major majority Serbian electorate and we could form the government without them according to the laws valid at the time. But we chose to divide the power with Muslims and Croats to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what you now tell us is that you're discussing the number -- the number of those functioning in the government was the issue, whereas a few lines later you say: "Whenever we would meet somebody would object to the fact that there are too many of them. It was too many for them, and for the Muslims and Croats, not enough." And then the next question was: "So you were aware that the creation of Republika Srpska did involve the deportation of Muslims and Croats?" And then you said: "Not necessarily. If the same hadn't happened at the other side." So the subject of the complaints made to you, where you first answered the question on ethnic cleansing, then continues about too many Muslims and Croats, and then develops into the direction of deportation. Was deportation not in any way mentioned when you had this meeting with Mr. -- one of these meetings with Mr. Karadzic and Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was deportation, used only once in Prijedor, and that was when a train was used, when I mentioned Ms. Korner in connection with this, a train could be used because the railway was operative at the time. Later on it stopped functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Please listen carefully to the question. The question was whether deportation was ever the subject of conversation in one of these meetings. Now you're explaining to us where the deportation took place, yes or no. But the question was whether it was the subject ever in such meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you seem to be making a fine distinction between deportations and expulsions. So deportations, as I understand it, refer to a kind of specifically organised train convoy that you observed from Prijedor on that occasion, as opposed to non-Serbs who were forced to leave the municipality under other -- to leave municipalities under other circumstances. In your view, is the question of deportation limited only to specific organised train convoys?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat again that trains could not be used for deportation or cleansing, because the trains were not operative. It was only in the very beginning of the war that they were operative. Now, whether they used trains, whether they used buses, they could have used planes. They also used planes for it, for people to leave. If you want me to specify what I mean by deportation, I'm referring to what had been done with the knowledge of Mr. Cornelio Sommaruga. The entire region was deported and the non-Serbs were moved out from the entire region, with the knowledge of Mr. Sommaruga and Rusa [phoen] Santo who was at the time chief of the International Committee of the Red Cross for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, that's deportation. And ethnic cleansing has nothing to do with the means of transportation, whether it's the train, it's the bus, or an aeroplane. What I want to say is: When you have large numbers of people leaving an area with the knowledge of Red Cross, that's what you call deportation, leaving aside ethnic cleansing. Here it says that the document was called "Voluntary moving out of the known Serbian population from Banja Luka," although basically it embraced the entire region.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was the subject of this exchange between you and Ms. Korner, that is, the departure of non-Serbs from Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did not really take in what I was saying. She was only interested in the wartime and in the period up to 1995, when there was the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. greatest exodus of the non-Serb population, carried out with the knowledge of Mr. Cornelio Sommaruga.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Radic, that you were explaining your view of some of the actors that affected the continued presence or departure of non-Serbs from Banja Luka, but the fact is that this discussion between you and Ms. Korner was about that subject, that is, the presence or departure of non-Serbs from Banja Luka; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's what the discussion was about. I explained to her why this came about, and the explanation -- that is, the text here says what the lady asked me and what my answer was. If you have 45.000 people arriving on the 15th of December, 1991 in Banja Luka, then you can't expect people of the -- non-Serbs to be left in peace, if you have had so many people who were expelled from Slavonia, 45.000 people, from Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And because of your efforts or your position on the subject, or at least the way others perceived your position on the subject, you were criticised that there were too many Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in July of 2001, you told Ms. Korner that that criticism occurred during a meeting or meetings between you, Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Krajisnik, when Mr. Karadzic said to you that Banja Luka hadn't been properly ethnically cleansed, that is, they were blaming you that there were still Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term of "ethnic cleansing" was used by Ms. Korner. At no point in time did I call it ethnic cleansing. Yes, I was criticised for it, because a large number of Serb refugees were in Banja Luka who had to be provided for.
