On the other hand, the Muslims and the Croats were also in Banja Luka, although they were in no better position than the Serb population, because they were jobless and all of these people had to be fed, had to be provided with medical care, children had to be taught at schools, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask one additional question, seek some clarification. If Ms. Korner would have asked you -- because I do understand that you are not satisfied with the words she used, ethnic cleansing. If she would have asked you whether during this meeting or such meetings you were blamed for a too-high remaining number of non-Serbs in Banja Luka and that, therefore, the expulsion had not been at a level they would have required, would you then have had less hesitations to say: Yes, that is what they blamed me for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They criticised me for the fact that, in addition to all the refugees coming in, there were such large numbers there, because they had to provide food and medicines, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but once they are there, I mean, what did they then expect you to do with that? To leave them -- that they would leave the area, that they would leave the territory, so that there was no need to feed them any more? Is that what they suggested, or what the one who spoke suggested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They probably had meant that the same should be done as did the other side that had expelled the Serbs and solved their problems that way, that is to say, the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then you are blamed for not having expelled non-Serbs, as Serbs were expelled from other territories, with, as a result, that there were too many non-Serbs remaining in Banja Luka who had to be fed and -- is that a correct understanding of -- and had to be given medical care? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've understood it well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what was said in meetings you had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Along those lines. Those were the suggestions made mostly. Nobody ever mentioned the methods of ethnic cleansing at all, which was suggested as having been conducted here, the suggestion made was that there was ethnic cleansing. Of course, I never would have accepted anything like that, any ethnic cleansing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, there was an occasion, was there not, on which you called Dr. Karadzic because a Jewish Slovenian family had been killed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first killing, especially the killing of the Jewish family, because if the wife is a Slovene, then you're a -- a Jew, then you're a Jew. The husband might have been a Slovene. And there was one working in the Municipal Assembly. As soon as I heard about that, the only person that I could call up, because I didn't have any reason to tell this -- to tell the police this, I phoned up the president, Mr. Karadzic, and told him to do anything he could, and everything he could, to issue orders that the killers be arrested. And within the space of three days, Inspector Bojic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he just said.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people were killed. Was a typical killing for benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- opportunistic killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether we have the interpretation in full. Could you please resume your answer on from where you said: "And within the space of three days, Inspector Bojic" and then what you -- what you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Arrested that group. He rounded them up and they were imprisoned. So the killers were known and the motive for the killing was known. It was for gain, for -- opportunistic, looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you indicated that the family was of mixed Jewish/Slovenian background. That was at least part of the -- of what prompted your call to Dr. Karadzic, isn't that right, because, as you've noted before, Serbs were very concerned when it comes to the suffering of the Jewish people because they always suffered as Serbs did; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there was an order from Dr. Karadzic, and within three days, everybody was arrested; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so when orders came from above, it was possible to investigate and arrests perpetrators of violent crimes in the Banja Luka area; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Although the ministry which was to have done that and was to have acted before President Karadzic, they should have done that. And if I might be allowed, Mr. Prosecutor, to say that I wouldn't have intervened with Mr. Karadzic, with President Karadzic, had the president of the Jewish community in Belgrade had let me know about the case that had taken place and asked for urgent intervention. Otherwise he said that he would transport all the Jews from Banja Luka to a hotel in Tel Aviv. And that's why I intervened with the president - to Tel Aviv, I'm sorry - to transport them to Tel Aviv, and that's why I intervened and said that this could lead to greater repercussions and unfortunate connotations with the international community and that is why the whole affair was dealt with very speedily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. I have no additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Get physically ready with a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's just to your right. It's not shared arms any more, but it's equality of arms, as far as the lectern is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, my name is Nicholas Stewart and I'm lead counsel for Mr. Krajisnik. You might have guessed some of that anyway already. Mr. Radic, you were a member of the SDS Main Board for a considerable period, and you --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you told the Court that you attended meetings of that Main Board?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on a regular basis, but yes, I did attend. Let me repeat: Not regularly, but I did attend them, and you can find that in the minutes and the records. You'll find exactly how many times I was absent for valid reasons. But yes, I did attend meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, from your own recollection, Mr. Radic, how many meetings of the Main Board did you say you attended all together?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult, Mr. Stewart, for me to give you an answer to that question. I don't have my own notes as to my attendance. But I do believe that the SDS archives have records and minutes and would be able to show you when I attended and perhaps even what I said on those occasions. But I myself can't remember the number now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How significant was your membership at the Main Board in your own overall political life in 1990, 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: The Prosecutor said that I was chosen as a non-party person, the SDS put me on his list -- on its list as a non-party person. And I thought that if I was on the SDS ticket, I should become a member of the SDS as well. And after that, I was elected as member of the Main Board. And it's a good idea that I was present and heard some of the things that were said at the Main Board myself. And finally, I was able to convey some of my attitudes and positions directly to the Main Board. That was a good thing. However, that did not mean that I used the party or would use the party to implement some of my own stands and positions. I had to adhere to the statute of the Municipal Assembly, the rules of procedure and the statute of Republika Srpska itself, because I was president of a legal body and not a political body, a legislative body and not a political body. So in that respect, it was a very good idea that I was at the source of all information. And I must also add that for about a year the SDS was put on ice, if you happen to lack that piece of information. The work of the SDS was put on ice. It was frozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And for what period do you say it was put on ice?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Krajisnik would be better placed to give you an answer to that, because I myself really wasn't at the Jahorina plenary session when the work of the SDS was resumed. But you'll be able to find the date, the exact date when the work of the SDS was put on ice, what the period of time was, when it started, and when it ended. I myself can't remember at this point. I think it was about a year, that the SDS did not function for about a year, and that is unprecedented that the party should put its own work on ice in wartime and not to act as a party on the ground or in the army either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, it's right, is it, when you think about it, that the period during which the work of the SDS was put on ice, as you've described it, included the whole of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1993, actually, but if you talk to your client, I'm sure you'll be given the exact date. Because I can't really remember the exact date when it was put on ice and when at the Jahorina plenary session their work was resumed. But it was about a year. And I think that was 1992, 1993, thereabouts, in the midst of the war. And that's what no party in Bosnia-Herzegovina could allow itself to do, because, quite simply, the ideological leadership, either in the army or the people, the political leadership, was just not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Radic, I'm sure you'll be delighted to know that Mr. Krajisnik and I do in fact talk to each other, but you are the one that's giving evidence. So try, as far as you can, please, to tell the Trial Chamber as much as you can recall and not worry about what Mr. Krajisnik and I might have to say to each other. So following my last answer, you have in fact been able to be a bit more specific in your recollection of the period during which the work of the SDS was put on ice. So could you try to be a bit more specific, then, in your recollection on this question, which is: When do you say was the last SDS Main Board meeting that you attended before the work of the SDS went on ice, in the way that you've described?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Not even approximately. All I know is that a piece of paper arrived to the Main Board, where it stated that the SDS work was put on ice, and that this led to astonishment on our part. Whether there was end of 1992, beginning of 1993, I really can't say. Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact, it was -- it could have been, and I'm putting to you it was, rather earlier, that it was actually around May, May 1992, that the SDS work was put on ice.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for that piece of information. I really couldn't remember myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, Mr. Radic, is that you know nothing to say that that's wrong; is that correct? You're not -- you wouldn't contradict that, whether you accept it or not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, and if you say you have a document saying that it was May 1992, then I'm willing to accept that. I can't say anything else. And that's it. Because I don't have the document, nor did I have a chance to discuss it with the Defence or the Prosecution before I came here. In the Brdjanin case, I did have contact with the Prosecution, but I'm coming here now and I don't know what I'm going to talk about, what you're going to ask me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is there any disagreement about the non-activity of the SDS starting in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I mean, I hesitate to be particularly precise, but in general terms, no, there's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then of course I wonder why we are spending a whole page of transcript ... Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, to answer Your Honour's wonderment, I don't know whether the Prosecution agrees something in advance and I'm also trying to get it clear, Your Honour, which is a legitimate -- cross-examination what this witness knows and what this witness remembers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- in an important area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, can you remember where you attended any Main Board meetings of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just the founders meeting, when the Main Board was selected, that took place in Sarajevo, because there were still Serbs in Sarajevo at the time, in the Djure Djakovica street, unless I'm mistaken. That's where that first founding meeting of the Main Board was held, and we could still walk around freely around Sarajevo at that time. Afterwards, when the parliament separated, then the headquarters moved to Pale, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So I'm going to press you, Mr. Radic, and invite you to think as hard as you possibly can about these events. Can you give some indication of the number of Main Board meetings that you attended before the parliament split, as you've described it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can remember is that I was called to Sarajevo to attend that particular meeting, when the Main Board was being chosen and elected and when I myself was elected to the Main Board. But I can't remember whether I attended meetings of the Main Board any more in that building that was assigned to us. That was already in 1991. I really can't remember that, whether there were other meetings held in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's get it straight. Is this right: That you don't have any positive recollection yourself of attending more than one meeting of the SDS Main Board in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Sarajevo, no. I can't remember. I can't remember attending more than one meeting. Now, if you were to jog my memory, I would be grateful to you. I was at another one in the Holiday Inn, but it wasn't the Main Board; it was a broader meeting, sometime in February, just before the war broke out. And I told the Prosecutor yesterday that I was ill, I had a bad cold, and that I left the meeting after the interval, the meeting held at the Holiday Inn. I think that was the last time that I ever went -- or that we ever met in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that was in February 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Just before the war, prior to the war. That was the last time that I was able to pass the turbe, because the Muslim guards were already there after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the move to Pale by the Bosnian Serbs, and I'm talking about -- I'm going to use the broad phrase "leadership" here or "the government of Republika Srpska." The move from Sarajevo to Pale, you know, do you, Mr. Radic, was in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of the war. I couldn't go down -- they couldn't go on being down below, so they had to go to the Serb area, to Pale. Because at Vraca, as I say, the first shot was fired in April at Vraca, after the rejection and withdrawal of Mr. Izetbegovic's signature from the Lisbon document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the answer is yes, you do know, Mr. Radic, that the Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- [Previous translation continues]... moved in April 1992 from Sarajevo to Pale? Yes, you do know that; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it couldn't have remained down there. It would have to have moved upwards, because the war began in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think I didn't hear the answer to your previous question, so I see that you've confirmed that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I instruct you: Mr. Radic, we have limited time. Very often you explain far more than what is asked. If Mr. Stewart would like to know further details, he'll certainly ask you about it. So therefore, could you please very much focus on the question put to you and only at the end of the questioning if you say there is an important or relevant part which was not asked of me which I would like to add, you can address me, but limit yourself to answers of the question. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, we're getting agreement. There's no problem about that. We're getting agreement about those events. So what you've described a few minutes ago about the need to be at Pale and the difficulties about being in Sarajevo, as far as Main Board meetings, any other meetings are concerned, that applies to the period after April 1992; that was the point at which it was no longer feasible to have meetings in Sarajevo, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then, as you have described it, there was the ice age, or there was the on-ice period for the SDS. So meetings that you attended in Pale after April 1992, those were some considerable time after April 1992, were they?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, for example, for the whole of the summer of 1992 - and I'd better define "summer" - from May 1992 through to September 1992, being optimistic about summer, you didn't go to Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I never went, but most probably I didn't, because if you say that it was already on ice, then this is July 1992. Because I haven't got the dates before me. I'm not quite sure about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There was in addition a real practical difficulty about getting from Banja Luka to Pale, wasn't there, through the period May, June, and into July 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dangerous. And I had to go through the corridor, through Brcko, on one occasion, and Prijedor [as interpreted] was just six or seven kilometres in width. I had to move along the Sava River and somebody could have shot at me from the Croatian side, so it was dangerous to go that way and I had to go right around. I couldn't take a short cut to Pale. So that is why I was absent on many occasions, because it was a very dangerous route and a very long one and exhausting one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think on the transcript, Your Honour, Prijedor -- sorry. Corridor has come across at Prijedor at page 58, line 6. That's a simple --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It makes sense and is logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said that on one occasion you had to go through the corridor, through Brcko. When was that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the corridor was expanded at Brcko and until the line -- the front line was stabilised. After the breakthrough of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm asking you when it was, as specifically as you can --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A breakthrough of the corridor took place on the 26th of June, 1992, and that's when the corridor expanded, became broader. On Vidovdan, the 26th, St. Vitus Day, the 26th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it was shortly before that, was it, this particular occasion when you went through the corridor.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were routes bypassing this, but it was a very dangerous route to take. Suljevica, Sokak, and so on. We had to pass through all these passages and goodness knows what to reach Zvornik and further upwards up the hill to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I realise these are complicated events at that time, but my question was rather more specific. I was asking you whether it was shortly before the breakthrough on the 26th of June that you, on that one occasion that you have mentioned, went through the corridor, moving along the Sava River, and so on.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just said that there was the route that we took even before the corridor was broken through. There was a path through the forest, a bypass, Trebava and that route so that's the route we took and did reach Pale that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to give up on that particular question, Mr. Radic. But what was the purpose of that visit to Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What purpose? Well, I was invited to come. Now, what the purpose was, I really can't say. I don't know. But I was up there. It wasn't that I wasn't there. It was the Main Board. Whether it was another kind of meeting up there. As I say, it was very rarely, because at the very dangerous to get up there. Now, what the purpose -- you want me to remember what the purpose was. I really can't. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You can't remember, Mr. Radic, then that's your answer. That is your answer. You having made this dangerous trip --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- To Pale, you nevertheless, and that's your answer, you simply can't remember why you went; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, no. Just as I can't remember most of the Main Board meetings, what the agenda was, what the subjects discussed was, what I said, what somebody said to me, and I really do not see that that -- well, my memory doesn't serve me that well after so many years, 12 years, in fact. And I haven't taken any notes with me, any papers with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So more generally, then, talking about meetings of the Main Board, leaving aside exactly when, where, how many, and so on, but meetings of the Main Board, you said -- you said previously in your evidence: "Those were meetings at which SDS policy was formulated." And that was your evidence. Could you give an illustration of a formulation of SDS policy that took place at a Main Board meeting at which you were present?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One such document was here on the desk, and now that I had the chance of reading it, I concluded that I would not have really discarded anything that we decided upon there. We were, first of all, establishing a system, because we had the municipalities that were taken on from the former system. We didn't have a government. We received all those orders that I was shown by Mr. Tieger here. And if I look at them now, I would not really distance myself from any of them, because we were talking about commodity reserves, stocks. Because the war had already started. We had to feed the people, give them medications, take care of the old and the young. And all of that you can read in these minutes that we had here, minutes from the Main Board meeting that was sent to all the municipal boards, that were then ordered to implement these decisions. And I would still stand by this document and sign it today, with a peace of mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could have -- it's P65. It's in binder 6, tab 66. It's a mystery. It's what has come to be known over many years as variants A and B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be grateful to you if you gave me my copy that I returned to you, where I scribbled some of my notes. I made a lot of annotations there, highlighted some parts. But if that can't be done ... But I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the slightest objection if it helps to the witness having that particular copy back. Obviously, he didn't hand it back to me, as it happens, but I have no objection whatever to that. I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question just is where that annotated document is. I haven't got any copy of your annotations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I received a copy and read it in my room there. I underlined certain things, made -- put my comments there, and it would facilitate and make things faster. But anyway, I can use this copy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could please do that, because we can't retrieve that. We usually do not save any personal copies as annotations. So if you have left it somewhere, it might not be available any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't want to deny your request, Mr. Radic, but it probably won't matter. I don't think it's going to hamper you or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, I just wanted to clarify: When you talked about a document a few minutes ago in your answer, that this is the document that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read this and I am familiar with it as a document. And now that I've read it once more, I've said that I would sign it again, I would put a seal on it, and I would stand by it. Because there's nothing in it that would point to anything harmful for other ethnicities. Quite the contrary; in several places, it says that care should be taken of these people, and this is the 19th of December, 1991, before the start of the war. This was a period when the Yugoslav People's Army had not been disbanded yet. But it concerns Bosnia and Herzegovina, and whatever it says about the mobilisation there, it talks about the mobilisation for the Yugoslav People's Army. So that if you have any specific questions arising from this document, I would like to listen to them very readily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's do that, Mr. Radic, shall we, and then if I do have -- I will have some specific questions, and then we can -- then you can deal with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, just on the question whether this was the document he was referring to, the witness took the opportunity to -- well, to take 15 lines. Could you please keep the witness to the questions you are putting to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect, I'm sure we can all do that. Your Honour is in a very strong position to do that as well as me. I will absolutely do my best, Your Honour. I will assist, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not have minded if you had interrupted the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's helpful, Your Honour, then, because I'm always -- well, I don't like to be too aggressive with the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I do understand. But this was a clear example of where you certainly could have done it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will aggress more, Your Honour, then, in that respect. Thank you for the invitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you talked about this document as a Main Board document, but it's already clear, isn't it: You did not yourself see this document at a Main Board meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And generally, is this the position: That you now, after a space of really many years, you have very little recollection, quite naturally, of what was said, what was done at particular meetings, unless on occasions your memory is jogged by looking at a document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really urge you to do that, to refresh my memory, by asking me a question, and I'll answer you. As for this particular document, I can tell you a lot about it, because it does contain very many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, we will do it perhaps in exactly the way His Honour suggests -- is that everything that you are going to tell the Trial Chamber about this document, if we could do it by my asking questions, and of course the Trial Chamber asking any questions it wishes to do, and you answering those questions. That would be a good way to proceed. The -- but the general point being that unless I do or somebody does put in front of you a document which you invite us to do -- to jog your memory, your actual recollection of, for example, discussions at Main Board meetings is, for practical purposes, zero, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without refreshing my memory, 10, 12 years later, it is difficult for me to talk about it without exposing myself to the risk of saying something that is not true or is not wrong [as interpreted], and that's really something I would like to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And this particular document, we call it Variant A and B, as a convenient shorthand, this particular document you get yourself in your evidence earlier, you get the link with the Main Board just from the fact that it says, top left-hand side on the cover page "Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina Main Board." That's right. That's the only basis of your link between this document and the Main Board, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There is another title and another cover, but that's -- I have nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But returning to the Main Board, then. The description that you've given so far rather suggests that the Main Board was concerned at meetings you attended with, if you like, establishing a structure, some mechanics, because it was all a new organisation. Is that the way you remember it or is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not wrong. That is something you can read in this document. That's the main part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said earlier in your evidence that -- and this is page 27 of yesterday's transcript. You don't have that, Mr. Radic, so don't -- I'm just helping others in court with the cross-reference. So don't worry about that. You said that you couldn't really say for a fact that this document, the one I'm calling Variant A and B, had reached all the municipalities, but you said "probably it did." And then the following page it was, page 28, you were asked about a meeting on or about December the 19th, 1991, and you said: "I don't recall being at this meeting at all, but having read this document here, I can see that this document was distributed to the municipal boards of the SDS, and that's when this so-called partisan document was then produced." So again, is this right: That you have actually no memory of such a document being distributed to the municipal board, no firsthand knowledge of it being distributed to municipal boards, plural, but that's the conclusion you draw from looking at the document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I look at this document and when I try to recall what had been done, and this is something that this document talks about, then I remember that the municipal board received this document, that it implemented it, and that we established the Assembly, the executive bodies, and many of the things stated here were actually carried out. This was a political document, an enactment for the creation of Republika Srpska, of its executive and legislative organs. I don't think that there are some parts of it that will be contrary to the protection of pregnant women or elderly, the manning of units according to the JNA quotas. Therefore, everything was functioning in accordance to the laws of the SFRY, including the army and everything else, and that's how it was proceeded. If there is any element here that you believe is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'll just stop you for a moment and return to this question. You said in your evidence earlier here: "Please believe me when I say that I don't recall receiving it." That's this document. So it appears clear that you yourself have no recollection of receiving this document back in 1991, 1992. That's right so far, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here "to all the municipal boards of the SDS," and the SDS municipal board is a political organisation that received the document and was tasked with implementing it in its territory. It did not go to the Municipal Assembly but to the municipal boards. And it says "strictly confidential," number, and so on and so forth. So why should I recall this since I wasn't the president of the SDS municipal board at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to make it clear for us, Mr. Radic, where precisely on the document that you're looking at it says -- you're getting that from within the text of the document, aren't you, that it went to all the municipal boards?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I don't have the text that I underlined, the other copy -- this was not sent -- well, it says "the SDS municipal board will immediately proceed to establishing the item 2, maintain the round-the-clock duty of all the SDS boards." And then you have Variant A, then the II. It says here that this was sent to them and that they were tasked with implementing this. Nowhere here does it read that we are to have anything to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just wanted to get it clear. The -- your inference from the document that it was sent to the SDS municipal boards is gleaned from the content of the document, because there are things to be done in connection with the composition of boards and their activities, you infer that it went to all those boards. That's the position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Because at the time, the municipal assemblies were not even established, sir. It says clearly here that the SDS candidates should be selected for the Municipal Assembly, its organs, and that government should be put in place, and so on, wherever it had not been already done. And that was a task for the municipal boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The question I asked you a couple of minutes ago, Mr. Radic, was to invite your confirmation that you have no actual recollection yourself, no actual memory in your head --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Memory of what, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, obviously he doesn't have no memory of anything at all in the world or his -- your life, Mr. Radic, so I should complete the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You anticipated it. I was asking you: No recollection or memory of having received this document. That I understood was the question you were anticipating.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A lot of the questions were about whether the Municipal Board received it and that's many --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to add that as well, then, Your Honour, since the -- in the light of the witness's anticipation, put it as two separate questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you also have no actual recollection yourself of anybody receiving this document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm inviting you to confirm that you have no actual recollection of anybody, Municipal Board, anybody, receiving this document.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that the SDS Municipal Board certainly did receive it, and I believe that the secretary of the Municipal Assembly also received all the documentation related to the establishment of government in Banja Luka. And I said that this document must be somewhere in the archives of the Municipal Assembly of the town of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, what I'm trying to get clear, because it's just a fairly -- it's a fairly basic point here that I'm trying to get clear. You have told the Trial Chamber, you've just told the Trial Chamber then, and you have told the Trial Chamber a few times, that you -- this document must have got to Municipal Assemblies, that it's your view that it did, that it's your inference or whatever. I'm asking you something much more specific. I'm asking you whether you can confirm that you yourself don't have any actual memory of this document being received by municipal board or anybody.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assert one thing, that the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, who was a lawyer, who was supposed to work on this and prepare it for the Assembly of the municipality, that he had to have received it. I did not have to receive it. It was the secretary and the Executive Board who were preparing material for the Assembly session who had to have received it. I was not suppose to receive it. But I wish to add once more that I do fully agree with everything that is stated contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you said in your evidence that -- you said: "I know that there was a discussion on this document." And then you gave your reason. But again, were you present at any discussion of this document in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did anybody report to you any discussion that they had had of this document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by what had been done, not only were discussions carried out, but many of the points stated therein were actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's a different point, Mr. Radic. We'll come to that in a moment. My question was more specific. It was whether anybody ever reported to you any discussion they had had of this document.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be frank, I do not remember whether anyone reported this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you yourself involved in the implementation of any of the matters which are directed, apparently, by this document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I take it in an order, these matters as they are stated here, or would you like me to respond to any specific matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd like us to start, Mr. Radic, by you answering my question, which is really just a yes or no, I invite you to accept, a yes or no as to whether you were yourself involved in the implementation of any of these matters, before we then go on to look at them separately.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And now you ask me, and then I'll tell you which points -- which matters were dealt by me and which by the SDS Executive Board. For instance, the first point here was dealt with by the Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading quickly. The interpreter couldn't catch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'm going to follow the course His Honour invited me to do which is to interrupt you, frankly, if you do not simply answer and stick to the questions which I'm asking, because I will have quite a lot of questions. So, if you answer all the questions I don't ask as well, we'll be here a very, very long time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you've now answered the question, saying that you were involved, and perhaps now Mr. Stewart will not let you explain who exactly was involved in what. But perhaps he's specifically interested in your own involvement in certain points. He might ask you questions about that. So the first response -- answer is quite clear. Listen to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've only got one question in this area maybe. We shall see where we go, Mr. Radic, but it is this: So it seems to follow - and confirm whether you accept that it does follow - that any involvement that you personally had in discussion, arrangement, implementation of any of the matters set out in this document were done with no reference whatever to this document; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if this is an instruction, how can I proceed without referring to this document? If a document states that we are supposed to do something, then whenever we do act upon it, we refer back to it. Because this seems to be a very general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'll perhaps be very plain about what is underneath my question and why I am suggesting to you that that is the position. You have really made it clear to the Trial Chamber on a number of occasions in your evidence that you did -- you do not recall ever seeing this document in 1991 and 1992. And then you tell the Trial Chamber that you were --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- involved in implementation of a number, and we needn't worry at the moment how many, but a number of items in this document. What I am suggesting to you, from a practical point of view, Mr. Radic, is it is just inconceivable that you and your colleagues were sitting around discussing the implementation of a number of matters in this document, with you having no recollection whatever of this document at all. It just makes no sense, does it, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have received many documents. And if I said that I did not remember this document, then it means I just do not remember it. I received a great many documents. But some of the matters mentioned herein were indeed implemented. Now, pursuant to what were they implemented, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, isn't this the position, without going through them too painfully, Mr. Radic: That there are a number of items in this document that would have made perfect sense to do in the situation if this document never existed? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- if that were not an unsuitable point for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would suit, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radic, we'll have a break for 20 minutes. We'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Radic into the courtroom. Mr. Radic, I'm aware that you asked again during the break whether the document where you made some annotations, that's the 19th of December, 1991 document, could be retrieved, but unfortunately it could not. So we have to do without. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, just looking at the copy of the document, then, that you have got, the same one we were looking at before, the instructions for the organisation and activity and so on, Variants A and B. Would you turn to the very last page, please. Do you see it says in typed letters, does it say "SDS Crisis Staff"? You're nodding.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Except in that sense, otherwise it's not signed, is it? Well, that's clear, isn't it? It's got no signature of any sort on it.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I be allowed to say something that I have been wanting to say for quite some time now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, as far as I'm concerned, you may answer my question freely. Beyond that, I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radic. You may say something you have already for a long time on your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A document of this document, we must bear in mind, which ends with the words Crisis Staff, SDS Crisis Staff, without a big stamp of the SDS, a round SDS stamp, and without the signature of the president of the Crisis Staff, if any body existed at the level of Republika Srpska in that capacity, that I am very wary towards any document of that kind, lacking those two things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single document that we received from the Main Board or from an organ of authority in Republika Srpska failed to have a stamp, a signature, and a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, asking for the obvious triggers these kinds of things, that it's without a tamp and without a signature, even if the witness would say it is a stamp and a signature on it, the Chamber might not accept this. It's obvious that there is no signature, there's no stamp. Is there any need to ask that to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, my next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do understand. I only say that asking for the obvious sometimes triggers these comments which -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you cast any light, Mr. Radic, on what might be meant in this document by "SDS Crisis Staff" on the last page?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that a secret procedure, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Forget about for the moment, unless it helps you to answer the question. I'm not concerned about the text above, apart from it being just the context of the whole thing. But specifically, the typed "SDS Crisis Staff," as if it were some kind of signature. I'm just putting it in those broad terms. Where it says SDS Crisis Staff, can you, from your knowledge, can you cast any light on what sort of -- what "SDS Crisis Staff" might be being referred to there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that an SDS Crisis Staff existed at the level of Republika Srpska. Had it existed, and knowing our weaknesses, the person who would be president of the Crisis Staff would certainly have signed such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- when you were interviewed in July 2001, you were -- page 80, this is, page 80. I don't think, Mr. Radic, you, for the moment, you needn't trouble about the actual document, but it's page 80, for the reference. You were asked by Ms. Korner: "Do you remember any kinds of instructions being received from or given by you because you were a member of the Main Board about the takeover of power in municipalities?" And I should say it's very clear here that Ms. Korner is asking you about this Variant A and B document. That comes very clearly from the previous page and the passage that's what it was all about. And your answer was: "There was nothing I could receive or issue, since the power was never taken over in Banja Luka. This probably referred to municipalities where, with a relative or absolute majority of non-Serbian population, it did not refer to Banja Luka." And then Ms. Korner put it to you: "It referred to both, didn't it? It referred to municipalities where there was a Serb majority and those where there was a Muslim majority?" And you answered: "What could they need? Why would they need it for those with a Serbian majority when by simple voting we had a majority in the Assembly? No measures were to be applied there because --" and then Ms. Korner says: "I'm asking you, when you saw this document, did you appreciate --" and so on. In fact I should say Ms. Korner seems to have been -- made an erroneous assumption there that you'd seen the document. But the -- is this right, Mr. Radic: That when you were being asked in the course of that interview and to -- it was specifically Ms. Korner at that point, about this document, that you didn't actually read through it before you answered those questions? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that. I said that in my previous answers, and I told Mrs. Korner loud and clear that we did not have any need to undertake any measures except those which were determined by the statute of the municipality, where it says, for instance, that if there was a majority number of deputies, they could set up government. So we had no need to snatch authority from anybody because we had the majority, the majority of Serb deputies, SDS ones, or those from the leftist parties, the communist, liberals, and so on and so forth, who supported the Serb majority. So we had no need to usurp anything or snatch anything from anybody. And we even gave the Muslims and Croats a certain number of seats in the executive organs. And as I've already said, the vice-premier was a Muslim, although according to the statute of the day, we were not duty-bound to give him that post. So we had no need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you can put that document on one side now, if that's convenient. We're not -- I'm not asking any more questions for the moment about that document. Then you were asked, and this is page 43 of yesterday's transcript, you were asked, with respect to the ARK Crisis Staff, you were asked: "Did that Crisis Staff receive instructions from above, instructions from Pale?" And your answer was: "It's difficult for me to answer that question. Most probably there had to have been some instructions, because it's difficult to imagine that Brdjanin himself would have made any decisions on his own." Do you say that Mr. Brdjanin never made any decisions on his own? I beg your pardon. You go on in that answer to say: "Although there were such decisions taken by him personally alone." And then you say: "There were also some decisions that were signed but not signed in his own hand." So can you indicate any decisions that you recall Mr. Brdjanin taking on his own?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, we mentioned a moment ago a case in point, when the professor, music professor from the school was dismissed. And then the case of the rector of the university. I drew his attention to the fact that the university rector could only be replaced by the university, which was autonomous. Unfortunately, he didn't listen to me. He didn't heed me. And we have the example of the former academician Samardzic from Belgrade that he would lose the possibility of having his diploma ratified before this had been solved. So this was one of the cases and instances in which Mr. Brdjanin did as he felt fit. I don't think anybody could have instructed him to replace or dismiss a rector, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then, same passage in your evidence yesterday, page 43. You had some evidence that you'd given in the Brdjanin case quoted to you, and you had an answer quoted to you: "Surely they must have obeyed the instructions that were coming from the republican government. That's for sure." And it was the regional authorities you were saying must have obeyed the instructions that were coming from the republican government. Then you said: "They had to receive instructions from someone about what they were supposed to do, and that someone was the republican authorities in Pale; correct?" Answer: "Someone from a higher level, naturally." And then just a tiny bit further on you say again: "I have to say that some things were done without the knowledge of the people from the top." Mr. Radic, when you talk about the republican authorities in Pale, you're talking in -- you're meaning, are you, to talk in very general terms about all the government offices and organs of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the executive organs, law-making organs that we had to respect and listen to. That's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that, for example, in relation to policing matters, you would most likely expect the instructions to come from the minister, minister of the interior, or whatever the precise phraseology would be, that was responsible for policing?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. That's what the case was before the war, during the war, and it's still like that now, that there is this subordination, the Ministry of the Interior down to the regional MUPs and the centres of security services within the centres of public security in towns, et cetera, so that not a single civilian organ of power and authority could wield any influence on them. Local civilian organs, like the president of the Municipal Assembly or someone like that. And not even the mayors of today; they couldn't do that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge yourself of any instruction coming either to the region or to your local municipality from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the one signed as an act enacted in the National Assembly. Otherwise, any other acts signed by Mr. Krajisnik, as president of the Municipal Assembly, I didn't have occasion to receive. I didn't receive anything else except, for example, greeting cards or a letter he might have sent. But he didn't write anything else, apart from the decisions made in the Assembly. If there's a document of that kind written by Mr. Krajisnik, then I'd like to ask you to show it to me. So I don't want it said or translated that I saw a document of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you aware of any such document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state now: If a document of that kind is in existence, I'd like to see it, but I can't remember of any such document being in existence by which Mr. Krajisnik made it incumbent on the president of the municipality, Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, to do anything. As to others, I don't know, but I personally didn't see a document of that kind ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Or in which Mr. Krajisnik made it incumbent on anybody to do anything; that's correct, isn't it? You have no awareness of any document coming from Mr. Krajisnik making it incumbent on anybody to do anything, apart from that Assembly document you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were decisions taken at the Assembly of a legislative order, and by virtue of that, they were signed by Mr. Krajisnik. And let me say straight away that it didn't come directly to me but to my secretary, the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, who then transformed it into the corresponding decisions of our Assembly if it had to do with us. So my secretary knows that, to matters of that kind far better than I do. I wasn't always kept abreast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you ever had a meeting between you and Mr. Krajisnik, just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just once, in the post-electoral campaign, in the year 2000, I think it was, when we discussed a possible coalition between my deputies and the SDS deputies. And I think on the occasion, Mr. Krajisnik -- no. No. That was in 1996, after the war. Otherwise, with Mr. Krajisnik, I did not have any separate meetings. Quite simply, according to the nature of his business, the work he did and the work I did, I didn't have any need to, because Banja Luka was full of deputies conveying what was happening over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever have any -- let's give it a time frame now. In 1990, 1991, and 1992, so let's say from multi-party elections up to the start of the war, let's say. Did you ever have any sit-down meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, and any other people, at which you were -- understand what I'm talking about by a sit-down meeting. I'm excluding any casual meetings or meetings where you run into each other in a corridor or chat in the course of an assembly session, something which is a meeting at which you are there to talk about something. Did you ever have any such meeting with Mr. Krajisnik and other people?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I saw Mr. Krajisnik for the first time at a rostrum when I was standing at the rostrum of the National Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we were all invited, all presidents of Municipal Assemblies were invited to attend the National Assembly. Unfortunately, I didn't have a meeting with him then or talk to him, and I doubt that Mr. Krajisnik even knew who I was at the time. He was the president of the National Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina until the split. I was president of the Municipal Assembly of the town of Banja Luka. So that was it. We never met alone during that period of time that you mentioned. I never had a meeting with him during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you've said a little bit earlier you had no meeting with him alone just the two of you, because I asked you specifically. But it seems, from the answer you've just given, that the slightly wider meeting at which there was you, Mr. Krajisnik, and other -- any other people, what you've just said applies to that. You never had any specific meeting of that type, including Mr. Krajisnik; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can even state quite certainly that even if we had a broader meeting with other people, it never had anything to do with any business, decisions, or anything like that. It was just -- happened to be a courteous exchange after some meeting. And I state once again that I never had a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik, any contact with him, nor did he with me, because, quite simply, the jobs were did were different so we didn't have any need to meet, except at meetings of the Main Board, of course, but then I did not have a meeting with him. I was there with all the members of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were asked in your evidence earlier in this case, and that was page 50 of yesterday's transcript, there had been discussions about the music teacher and so on and then you were asked about orders in relation to what was euphemistically called differentiation of personnel that might have come from Pale. And you were asked: "These balancing orders or differentiation of personnel orders, these dismissals, came from Pale; is that right, came from the very top?" And you said: "I don't know if this term of differentiation of personnel was used or not, but although I know -- I don't know where it originates from, that is, but I know that it was indeed applied at the municipal level under such a name." And then you were asked: "And with that clarification, is it correct that the orders for that to be applied at the municipal level came from the very top, came from Pale?" Then you said: "They did not. They did not come from the very top but from the level immediately superior to us, to the municipality. There were maybe one or two instructions that arrived directly from the top, but not more than that." Given that there's a maybe in your answer anyway there, Mr. Radic, but when you say there were maybe one or two instructions that arrived directly from the top, do you have any recollection at all of what any such instructions might have involved?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do is to assume what it said, what was written. I cannot assume, nor can I say with any certainty, who sent it. However, that went through a transformation, and it happened not only to music teachers, but, as I said yesterday, to people of Serb ethnicity who weren't members of the SDS and who didn't want -- who they didn't want to dismiss. So I said that with the intervention of President Karadzic, this was stopped and the question was never raised again. Now, what do you mean that somebody had -- which means that somebody probably created or came by a decision of that kind at the level of the Crisis Staff on his own. So I didn't see a document of that kind, but I assume that it would have said that the Serbs too, that it applied to Serbs too, who weren't members of the SDS, that they should be replaced from managerial posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so far as you were asked in your evidence yesterday, page 55, Mr. Tieger said: "First of all, I indicated I would direct your attention to portions of the interview." And that's the July 2001 interview, in which you indicated two different reasons why you knew and concluded that the balancing instructions, and we explored that this morning. That's again the euphemistic label of balancing instructions in relation to dismissals of non-Serbs. Indicated two different reasons why you knew and concluded that the balancing instructions came from Pale. And then let me focus on the first one. Did you indicate on -- in July 2001 one of the reasons why you knew they had come from Pale was that the instructions were implemented all over Republika Srpska? Correct. And did you indicate that an additional reason why you knew that was because there was a document which was brought to the Crisis Staff in order to be implemented, a document from Pale referring to the balancing? I don't know because I didn't see the document. Quite possibly, I said that a document existed; however, I never saw such a document about this balancing business. I just want to be clear, Mr. Radic. Is this the position: You simply do not know whether there was or wasn't such a document? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You gave some evidence about -- well, the position is this: We explored this a bit. Banja Luka was very cut off from the beginning -- early in the war, April 1992, through to -- and you've given the date, at the end of June, I think you said, the 26th of June. But whether it was late June, early July, over that period, Banja Luka was very cut off from -- well, certainly from Pale, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very dangerous, but we did find a route to reach Pale, although it was very risky. But it is true that in the Brcko area, it was cut off. There was the army there, hostile to the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, to the point where for a considerable period, there was not even telephone communication between Banja Luka and Pale; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And for how long was telephone communication cut off?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the liberation, so to say, of the corridor, until the passage was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Starting when? So what was the -- overall. Precise number of days doesn't matter, Mr. Radic, but how long do you recall telephone communication being cut off between Banja Luka and Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that it was on the 26th of June in 1992 that the telephone lines were connected, reconnected. Now, when they were cut off with Serbia and Pale, it's very difficult to say. Different methods were used to restore the communication lines, not to have it discontinued. There were military lines that were used for those purposes, in order for us to receive and send information, that is, between us and Pale, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you referred in evidence yesterday, and this is page 62, to a deputy, an Assembly deputy in Prijedor having had a radio set to report regularly to Pale what was happening in Prijedor, are you talking about that period immediately before 26th of June, when telephone communications were cut off?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly. I don't recall when it was that he had it, but I recall his colleagues from Prijedor and around telling me that he had the radio set and that he was keeping in touch. But I don't know when it was. But the deputy involved was one of the most senior deputies in the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you'd agree with this rather obvious proposition, wouldn't you, Mr. Radic, that if there were telephone communications between Prijedor and Pale, a radio set would hardly have been a matter of any great significance or extra value, would it? That's obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many things are obvious. The important matter is whether he had the radio set in that particular period of time. If he did, that's quite understandable. Because I, for my part, had to go to the army to ask them to help me establish communication lines with Pale, which they did, in order for me to know what was going on and what I was supposed to do. Therefore, there were no communication lines and it was very dangerous to use wires, because they could easily be cut off. But I noticed that telephone conversations were intercepted even in the period of time when these lines weren't functioning as well as they should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you said you had to go to the army to ask them to help you establish communication lines with Pale in order for you to know what was going on and what you were supposed to do, when was that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was also in the period subsequent to this one, when certain lines had to be maintained that were not supposed to be deciphered. They had to be secure. And in this way, we made sure that we could communicate with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last word the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I'm going to have to just invite you to, if you can, to just repeat your last sentence. It wasn't picked up by the interpreter. You said: "They had to be secure. In this way we made sure we could communicate --" something or other.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the top, with the leadership. Right. This was also the practice later on when the lines were resumed, when the corridor was made passable, that we would use these special lines for information that was of confidential nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when is the first time that you went to the army to ask them to help you establish communication lines with Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the date, but I can tell you that up until the 26th, this was the only way I could maintain communication. But it is very difficult for me to say when it was for the first time that I used this method to keep up communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was after the beginning of April 1992, was it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the corridor was cut off. As soon as the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina cut off the route there, that was when the lines went down as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was that request that you made -- well, where did you go? What army establishment did you go to to make that request?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the only army that was in existence, and that was regular, and that was the Yugoslav People's Army. That was still the Yugoslav People's Army. It was there. Later on it became the Army of Republika Srpska. As soon as the war broke out on the 15th of May, the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew, the Army of Republika Srpska was established. Those members of the JNA who wanted to stay there, stayed there; others withdrew. And those were the two armies that we could appeal to to let us use their lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said you went to make that request for them to establish communication for you. But was that line of communication that you've asked to be established to Pale, was that for you and other colleagues of yours?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't happen as often, you know. Only when the situation was very urgent for me, when I had to get in touch with them, when they had to get in touch with us. But you couldn't use the army all the time, because they had to guard their secure lines. It was wartime. Everybody was spying on everybody else, intercepting lines in order to find out what was going on. Therefore, we did not use them as often. But, fortunately, this situation did not prevail for that long, because on the 26th, the corridor was made passable and that's when we could resume, re-establish the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, can we get a couple of specifics clear, then. It was on each separate occasion that you wanted to communicate that you went and made a request to the army, and on each specific occasion they would help you out with that? Is that the correct picture?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They helped us to keep in touch through their lines, to keep in touch with the top. Therefore, not -- it wasn't through the army itself; it was by using their communication lines that we would establish contact. And as I said, it lasted for some two months, as long as the blockade lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to get it clear. I mean, perhaps this is a trivial illustration, but I hope it will make it clear. It's as if you were home and your telephone line has gone down for some reason and then from time to time when you want to make a call you go to one of your neighbours and ask to use their telephone and they allow you to do it. It was that sort of arrangement rather than the army providing you with some general continuing facility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would not give us these facilities at all. Whenever we requested this from them, they would allow us to use them. But, of course, they preferred that we use it as infrequently as possible, because they did not really look upon it favourably that we would come so often there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How often did you go during the period up to June 26th?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot say, but very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Once, twice, five times? It was a period of two or three months.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us say five times, although the period was from April until the 26th of June. The recommendation was: Don't use it very often, but only when in dire need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you ever use -- it was telephone, was it, they provided you with? Telephone or radio? It was telephone, was it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever they had at their disposal, they provided to us. They had their own lines. You had satellite telephones at the time. Everything was there. What the particular line was that they gave us to use, I'm not an expert, I cannot say, but I did keep in touch, just as I kept in touch with the secretariat for the implementation of measures against Yugoslavia when those 12 babies were dying on me, and that was the only way I could establish contact with the United Nations. Unfortunately, it was to no use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you used the -- or when you obtained the army's help to communicate with Pale -- well, perhaps I should ask you this. You said just a few occasions and a figure of five as a very rough figure was put on it. Are we talking, then, and those, if they were five occasions, but on those occasions, are we talking about communication only with Pale or with other places as well?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been too much for me to keep in touch with Sanski Most, Prijedor, this way, when I could have gotten into a car and gone there. It was with Brcko that I should have gone to, and then with Zvornik, there was no need for me to really keep in touch with them that much. As for the rest, I could always have used the car to go and talk to them directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, may I again instruct you to answer the question. The question was whether these telephone facilities put at your disposal by the army were used only for contacts with Pale or with anyone else. I take it from your answer that it's a simple: Just for Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only for the top leadership. For the rest, it wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That means only for Pale, does it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever on those occasions, did you ever have any direct communication with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you referred in your interview in July 2001, and then it's been discussed again in the course of your evidence here, to Mr. Krajisnik as a masterful leader that -- it sounds, and was that intended by you, Mr. Radic, as complimentary?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that Mr. Krajisnik was a powerful leader. He was president of the National Assembly, respected by the deputies, and whatever the documents he sent me, I implemented them. And this was something that was said by Ms. Korner. I said that I would never talk about him in those terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just wondered whether the witness was answering the question as if it would have said powerful leader, where the words were different. Perhaps you could confront the witness with the -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
